newsitem.title: USA: Internet consumer privacy initiative gets backing.
newsitem.headline: Internet consumer privacy initiative gets backing.

text.p: A group of computer makers, software developers, telecommunications companies, retailers and publishers are backing an initiative to preserve consumer privacy and avoid government regulation of the Internet.

The initiative will be announced Tuesday. Called TRUSTe (formerly known as eTRUST), it is a non-profit, industry-driven organisation based in Palo Alto, Calif and working to promote electronic commerce by protecting consumer privacy and staving off regulation.

TRUSTe hopes to assure consumer privacy on the Internet by alerting consumers to the uses of their personal information through the use of "trustmarks" or logos posted on Web sites that tell them how the information will or will not be used.

The organisation, whose partners include such heavy hitters as AT&T Corp. and International Business Machines Corp., was formed last July and in October formed a partnership with the CommerceNet consortium to implement its initiative.
TRUSTe will announce Tuesdday the commercial availability of its programme to use its branded trustmarks, which tell an individual how their information will be used.
Companies can license the trustmarks for a licensing fee, which ranges from $500 to $5,000, depending on the size of the company and the sensitivity of the information.

The trustmarks tell a consumer that the information they reveal online will: 1) not be used by the Web site they are visiting; 2) is collected only by the site's owner for its use; or 3) is collected and provided to third parties but only with the user's knowledge and consent.
"It's akin to a 'Good Housekeeping Seal' online," said Susan Scott, executive direcor of TRUSTe. "People are two to three times more likely to give information online if they know the use."

Scott also pointed to a study in March by The Boston Consulting Group, which said that concerns about privacy of personal information on the Internet is a consistent and significant concern for consumers online.

The Boston Consulting Group reported that in a survey, over 41 percent of respondents report leaving Web sites when asked to provide registration information over the Internet. Another 27 percent provide false personal data.
The Boston Consulting Group estimated that as much as $6 billion in additional electronic commerce revenues could be gained by the year 2000 if privacy issues were addressed.
"We want the trustmarks to be ubiquitous throughout the Net," Scott said. "The consumer should have a choice."
TRUSTe said it will monitor its licensed Web site publishers to ensure the proper use of their trustmarks.

In addition to AT&T and IBM, TRUSTe's partners include Oracle Corp, Tandem Computers Inc., Wired Ventures, the privately held publisher of Wired magazine; Netscape Communications Corp., Lands' End Inc., CyberCash Inc. and many others.
